Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Modern economies have become so profoundly interdependent that no single nation's markets can be understood in isolation. --- INTERDEPENDENCE (n) = sự phụ thuộc lẫn nhau; thường dùng dạng tính từ "interdependent" sau "become/render"; collocation "economic interdependence".

2. Some governments have resorted to protectionism, imposing heavy tariffs on imported steel to shield local manufacturers from foreign competition. --- PROTECTIONISM (n) = chủ nghĩa bảo hộ mậu dịch; tính từ đi kèm là "protectionist" (protectionist tariffs), không phải "protectionism tariffs".

3. A handful of superpowers still maintain hegemony over global trade negotiations and set the rules that smaller nations must follow. --- HEGEMONY (n) = quyền bá chủ, sự thống trị; collocation "global/economic hegemony", "challenge the hegemony of".

4. Many electronics firms have engaged in offshoring, relocating their assembly lines abroad to cut labour costs, even though this means fewer factory jobs at home. --- OFFSHORING (n) = chuyển sản xuất/dịch vụ ra nước ngoài; phân biệt với "outsourcing" (thuê ngoài, có thể vẫn trong nước).

5. The disparity in income between wealthy and poor nations has widened sharply since trade barriers began falling. --- DISPARITY (n) = sự chênh lệch lớn; luôn hàm ý so sánh giữa hai bên; collocation "widening disparity", "income disparity".

6. After years of relying on overseas factories, several car makers are now pursuing reshoring, bringing production back to their home countries. --- RESHORING (n) = đưa sản xuất trở về nước sở tại; đối lập với "offshoring"; viết liền không gạch nối.

7. International organisations are working hard to eradicate extreme poverty within a generation. --- ERADICATE (v) = xoá bỏ hoàn toàn, tận diệt; dùng cho vấn đề nghiêm trọng (poverty, disease), không dùng cho mức giảm nhẹ.

8. Fund managers are pouring capital into emerging economies like Vietnam and Indonesia, hoping for high returns. --- EMERGING (adj) = mới nổi, đang phát triển nhanh; collocation cố định "emerging economies/markets".

9. To reduce overheads, the airline turned to outsourcing, hiring an external company abroad to handle all its customer-service calls. --- OUTSOURCING (n) = thuê ngoài; nếu ra nước ngoài cụ thể thì gọi là "offshore outsourcing".

10. Critics argue that global fast-food chains and shopping malls are driving the homogenisation of cities everywhere. --- HOMOGENISATION (n) = sự đồng nhất hoá, mất bản sắc riêng; chính tả Anh-Anh dùng "-isation"; collocation "cultural homogenisation".

11. Decades of trade liberalisation have opened domestic markets to fierce foreign competition. --- LIBERALISATION (n) = sự tự do hoá thương mại/kinh tế; collocation "trade/market liberalisation"; chính tả Anh-Anh "-isation".

12. Rather than a bilateral deal between just two countries, this new trade pact is multilateral, involving more than a dozen nations negotiating together. --- MULTILATERAL (adj) = đa phương, liên quan từ ba bên trở lên; đối lập với "bilateral" (song phương).
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: A lot of manufacturing has shifted to developing countries where labour is considerably cheaper.
Band 8: Offshore outsourcing enables firms to slash labour costs, albeit at the expense of local employment in their home markets.
2. Band 7: Trade disputes between nations can sometimes escalate into serious diplomatic conflict rather than fostering cooperation.
Band 8: Far from guaranteeing harmony, trade frictions can just as readily precipitate diplomatic conflict as they can cement mutual interdependence.
3. Band 7: Workers in developing nations are sometimes subjected to unfair and exploitative treatment by multinational corporations.
Band 8: Multinational corporations frequently exploit lax labour laws, resulting in exploitative labour practices that leave workers in developing nations acutely vulnerable.
4. Band 7: Many highly skilled professionals leave poorer countries in search of better-paid opportunities overseas.
Band 8: The severe brain drain deprives emerging economies of their most talented professionals, who are lured abroad by markedly better prospects.
5. Band 7: Because instant global communication connects everyone, the world increasingly resembles one closely knit community.
Band 8: With the internet connecting us instantly, it truly is a global village, in which geographic distance scarcely impedes the flow of information.
6. Band 7: Some countries have deliberately begun to separate their economies from rival powers for political reasons.
Band 8: Decoupling is no longer merely rhetorical; strategic disentanglement from rival economies is now being pursued as a matter of deliberate policy.
7. Band 7: Small local businesses find it difficult to compete fairly against huge multinational corporations.
Band 8: Small domestic businesses desperately need a level playing field if they are to compete on anything approaching equal terms with multinational giants.
8. Band 7: A single smartphone is typically designed in one country, built from components manufactured in several others, and finally assembled somewhere else entirely.
Band 8: A modern smartphone illustrates a global value chain: designed in one country, with components fabricated across several others and final assembly undertaken elsewhere still.

passages.text: The image of global manufacturing as a finely tuned just-in-time machine — components arriving from distant suppliers on the precise day they are needed — dominated business writing for two decades before a series of disruptions cast doubt on the model. Researchers have since revisited the question of how much resilience can be built into international supply chains without forfeiting the cost advantages that made offshoring attractive in the first place. The institutional vehicle most often discussed is the partial reshoring of strategic components, including semiconductors, advanced pharmaceuticals and electric-vehicle batteries. The story matters because the answer shapes industrial policy, employment patterns and the cost of finished goods.

Three broad positions dominate the current literature. The first, defended by Professor Daniela Brunetti of Bocconi University in Milan, argues that the experience of the 2020-2022 disruptions has been over-interpreted by policy-makers. Brunetti's 2023 analysis of trade-flow data across thirty-eight industries indicates that roughly seventy-four per cent of the supply shocks observed in that period were resolved within nine months by ordinary market substitution, without explicit reshoring intervention. The second position, associated with Dr Mateo Ferreira of the Inter-American Development Bank, emphasises the strategic exception. Ferreira's group has documented that a small number of components, including a handful of semiconductor categories and several critical pharmaceutical inputs, exhibit concentration patterns severe enough that any reasonable definition of national security would treat them as a separate case. Ferreira concedes that broad reshoring is rarely cost-effective but argues that the strategic exception deserves a dedicated policy framework rather than being folded into general industrial policy.

A third position is offered by Professor Naoko Hashimoto, an economist at Hitotsubashi University in Tokyo. Hashimoto accepts the descriptive findings of both her colleagues but argues that the more interesting question is geographical. In a 2023 mixed-methods study covering one hundred and forty-six manufacturers across Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, her team traced how firms in those economies have responded to recent disruptions by diversifying suppliers across multiple countries within Asia rather than by relocating production to their home markets. The pattern, she suggests, depends less on reshoring in the narrow sense than on what trade economists now call "friend-shoring" — the deliberate clustering of suppliers across politically aligned jurisdictions. Where such clustering is in place, supply resilience tends to improve without significant cost penalty; where the response defaults to home-market relocation, average unit costs tend to rise by between nine and seventeen per cent.

Not all researchers accept the optimistic readings. Critics, including Dr Yusuf Adesina of the African Centre for Economic Transformation in Accra, have argued that the resilience literature has so far paid too little attention to the costs imposed on lower-income exporting economies. Adesina's group reviewed thirty-one reshoring announcements by European and North American firms and found that fewer than half came with transition support for displaced suppliers in lower-income economies. He does not deny that resilience matters for importing countries, but insists that the distributional consequences of partial reshoring should be treated as part of the analysis rather than as an externality, particularly where the displaced suppliers depend on a small number of contracts for a substantial share of national export earnings.

What the four accounts share, despite their differences, is a preference for treating supply-chain redesign as a question of selective intervention rather than wholesale relocation. Brunetti's market-substitution evidence works best when paired with Ferreira's strategic-exception framework. Hashimoto's friend-shoring findings work best when paired with Adesina's distributional caution. The most carefully designed studies, the literature suggests, treat reshoring as one option among several, even though political pressures often push governments to announce headline programmes that imply more than the evidence supports.

Some implications for policy follow. Several jurisdictions have introduced targeted subsidies, including the United States CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 and the European Chips Act of 2023, both of which focus on semiconductors rather than reshoring across all industries. Early evaluations from independent analysts suggest moderate progress on capacity targets and limited movement, so far, on the price gap that originally drove offshoring. Whether these instruments will broaden into wider reshoring policy or remain narrowly targeted depends, in Hashimoto's view, on whether the political appetite for the necessary public investment outlasts the supply-shock memory.

By no means does this imply that the resilience question is settled. The evidence base is uneven across regions, the sample of disruption episodes since 2020 is small, and the longer-term effects of friend-shoring on innovation and consumer prices remain a matter of debate. The aim of the more thoughtful research, the literature suggests, is not to declare globalisation obsolete but to identify the conditions under which selective resilience measures can be sustained without recreating the very vulnerabilities they were intended to address.

A related point concerns timing. Several economists have observed that the political salience of resilience tends to fade quickly once visible disruptions subside, and that subsidy programmes designed during a crisis may be poorly suited to the years that follow. If the underlying analysis is correct, then the more interesting policy question is not whether to act during a shock but how to design instruments that survive the calm intervals between shocks. Hashimoto's view, that the political appetite for the necessary public investment must outlast the supply-shock memory, captures the central difficulty.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we're hearing from Yuki and Mateo on quantitative trade-history methodology. Yuki, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname for me?

Yeah, sure. So I'm Yuki Tanabe-Smith — that's T-A-N-A-B-E hyphen S-M-I-T-H, one hyphen, no apostrophe. My project was a longitudinal study reconstructing trade-flow elasticities across forty-two port-city dyads in the long nineteenth century. (Q1)

Erm, the pilot ran in 2019 — sorry, no, 2018 — and the main wave concluded in 2022. So four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2021, but the archive-access permissions, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Tense-wise, just to clarify for the recording — your data-construction FINISHED in 2022, you're publishing this year, and the comparative wave starts when?
Published 2026, and the next comparative wave we're gonna run starts in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens here is what Friedrich Achebe-Olsen called the "asymmetric-gains framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: unequal exchange, dependency-trade theory, core-periphery accounting. All those describe overlapping phenomena. The current scholarly term, though, is asymmetric gains. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Yuki's framing. In my sample — twenty-six port-pairs across Atlantic and Pacific routes — most of the port-pairs showed asymmetric volume capture in favour of the metropole AT LEAST three times the periphery's share. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — twenty out of twenty-six, so roughly seventy-seven per cent. Only a few — about eight per cent — showed near-symmetric flows, and some — fifteen per cent — produced mixed or context-dependent ratios. (Q4)
Right. Now, Yuki, did your sample confirm the "tariff-determines-trade-volume" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the port-pair dyads I observed did NOT exhibit a deterministic volume response to tariff shifts. The institutional infrastructure, well, matters more. Today's economic historians treat tariff schedules as one input among many, not the master variable. Only a small minority — fewer than fifteen per cent — of dyads showed a clean tariff-elasticity signature. (Q5)

And, dunno about you, but I found something interesting on the credit-network axis. So-called clearinghouse concentration — where two or three London bills-of-exchange houses cleared the bulk of inter-imperial flows — that's actually rising sharply in the 1860-1890 window. And the literature suggests this constrained smaller ports' capacity for autonomous price-setting.
Hmm. Yuki, did you control for currency stratum?
Kinda. We stratified by gold-standard quartile. Counter-intuitively, the BOTTOM quartile — the late-adopters — reported the highest volume-growth velocities, not the early adopters.
Well, it's about catch-up substitution — undervalued currency made their exports cheaper, so trade partners leaned on them harder.

And one final thing — shipping-time data. In smaller port-pairs with under three thousand kilometres separation, freight-rate volatility was, um, considerably higher than in long-haul pairs over six thousand. Researchers attribute it to scarcity of redundant routing capacity.

Right. Now, going back to what Yuki mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Mateo, on your seventy-seven-per-cent figure: the implication that asymmetric capture was the systemic norm aligns with Achebe-Olsen, but Yuki's tariff-elasticity finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: The two maps depict the reconfiguration of a Western electronics multinational's supply-chain network between 2010 and 2024, charting the location of its manufacturing hubs, assembly plants and component flows.

Overall, the network underwent a pronounced geographical contraction. Chinese capacity was substantially reduced, whereas North American and Indian footprints expanded, indicating a deliberate shift away from concentrated offshoring toward a more regionalised model.

In 2010, four of the firm's six manufacturing hubs were clustered in China, supported by single hubs in Vietnam and Mexico and two assembly plants in Malaysia and Poland. Components were shipped along long trans-Pacific routes to consumer markets in the USA, Europe and Japan.

By 2024, however, only two Chinese facilities remained, both visibly downsized, while new hubs had emerged in Texas, India and an expanded Mexican site; a third assembly plant had also opened in Arizona. The component flows transformed accordingly, with the long-haul trans-Pacific arrows giving way to compact regional clusters spanning North America, Southeast Asia and the EU. This restructuring, arguably driven by geopolitical risk, suggests a clear prioritisation of resilience over the lowest-cost option.

The flows contracted in tandem, the trans-Pacific routes giving way to three compact regional clusters around North America, Southeast Asia and the EU. That the firm should reshore even as costs rose suggests a recalibration in which resilience, not cost minimisation, now governs the global value chain.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although critics blame globalisation for job losses in developed nations, automation and technological change have arguably displaced far more workers than the relocation of factories abroad.
While protectionist tariffs are intended to shield vulnerable industries, they frequently raise costs for domestic consumers and invite retaliatory measures that harm exporters in turn.

Although multinational investment is sometimes accused of exploitation, it also brings foreign direct investment, infrastructure and technical know-how that can raise living standards in host economies.

Automation is likely to reduce the labour-cost advantage that once drove offshoring, potentially reversing decades of production migration to low-wage economies.
Digital platforms are expected to accelerate the liberalisation of trade in services, allowing even small firms to reach customers across the globe with minimal overhead.
Emerging economies are projected to command a growing share of global trade and investment, gradually reshaping institutions that have long been dominated by established powers.

blocks.text: Whereas free trade tends to maximise overall economic output,
Developed economies generally possess the capital and technology to weather trade shocks, whereas emerging economies remain far more vulnerable to sudden shifts in global demand.
Reshoring production tends to raise consumer prices compared with offshoring, though it offers greater supply security in return.
Cultural exchange fostered by globalisation contrasts sharply with the homogenisation it can also produce, as unique local traditions risk being displaced by dominant global brands.
A hypothetical developing nation that opens its markets too abruptly might see local manufacturers collapse under competition from established multinational rivals within a matter of years.
An emerging economy that successfully attracts sustained foreign direct investment can illustrate how global trade, if properly managed, translates into new infrastructure and rising employment.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: For four decades, globalisation has been hailed as a process that benefits everyone, yet a growing number of analysts argue that the gains have flowed disproportionately to wealthy nations. While there is real evidence of unequal benefits, I disagree that developing economies have been net losers, although the picture is undeniably mixed.

Those who support the critical view marshal compelling arguments. Multinational corporations have repeatedly relocated production to poorer countries to exploit lax labour laws, paying minimal wages while extracting substantial profits for headquarters in wealthier nations. It is the unequal terms of trade that, in their view, lock developing nations into low-value exports such as raw materials and basic textiles, which tends to entrench rather than narrow the income disparity. Furthermore, cultural homogenisation often erodes indigenous heritage as Western brands flood emerging markets.

On the other hand, the headline gains for developing countries are too large to dismiss. Hundreds of millions of people in East and Southeast Asia have escaped absolute poverty as a direct result of integration into global supply chains. Foreign direct investment has built modern infrastructure, transferred technology and created jobs that pay above local averages. What countries like Vietnam, India and Bangladesh have demonstrated is that strategic engagement with global trade can dramatically accelerate development, provided that domestic institutions are reasonably competent.

In conclusion, although globalisation has clearly produced winners and losers within every economy, the suggestion that it has benefited rich nations at the expense of poor ones tends to oversimplify a complex record. What developing countries require is fairer trade rules and a more level playing field, rather than a retreat from global engagement itself.

That globalisation has redistributed wealth on a planetary scale is uncontroversial; whether it has done so at the systematic expense of developing nations is far more contentious. Having weighed the evidence, I disagree with the strong version of the claim: while gains have plainly been uneven, the assertion that poor nations have been net losers does not survive scrutiny.

Critics raise serious points. Trade liberalisation has frequently locked developing economies into low-margin segments of global value chains, while multinational corporations exploit regulatory arbitrage to suppress wages and externalise environmental costs. So pronounced has this asymmetry been that some economists describe contemporary trade as a form of neo-colonial extraction. Moreover, the cultural hegemony of Western media risks homogenising indigenous traditions, eroding the soft power of smaller nations. None of these concerns is trivial.

Nevertheless, the macro-level record complicates the indictment. Roughly a billion people have moved out of extreme poverty since 1990, the bulk of them in countries that aggressively pursued export-led integration. What economies such as South Korea, Vietnam and Botswana illustrate is that, with competent industrial policy, globalisation can serve as a ladder rather than a trap. Recent trends only reinforce this point: the wave of reshoring and selective decoupling now sweeping advanced economies threatens precisely those developing nations that depend on access to Northern markets, which suggests that globalisation, far from being uniformly extractive, has long been a vital channel of upward mobility.

On balance, then, globalisation's benefits and harms are mediated by domestic institutions and bargaining power, not destiny. What the international system genuinely requires is fairer rules - on tax, intellectual property and climate finance - rather than withdrawal. Reform, not retreat, offers the most credible route to a more equitable global economy.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Modern economies have become so profoundly interdependent that no single nation's markets can be understood in isolation. --- INTERDEPENDENCE (n) = sự phụ thuộc lẫn nhau; thường dùng dạng tính từ "interdependent" sau "become/render"; collocation "economic interdependence".

2. Some governments have resorted to protectionism, imposing heavy tariffs on imported steel to shield local manufacturers from foreign competition. --- PROTECTIONISM (n) = chủ nghĩa bảo hộ mậu dịch; tính từ đi kèm là "protectionist" (protectionist tariffs), không phải "protectionism tariffs".

3. A handful of superpowers still maintain hegemony over global trade negotiations and set the rules that smaller nations must follow. --- HEGEMONY (n) = quyền bá chủ, sự thống trị; collocation "global/economic hegemony", "challenge the hegemony of".

4. Many electronics firms have engaged in offshoring, relocating their assembly lines abroad to cut labour costs, even though this means fewer factory jobs at home. --- OFFSHORING (n) = chuyển sản xuất/dịch vụ ra nước ngoài; phân biệt với "outsourcing" (thuê ngoài, có thể vẫn trong nước).

5. The disparity in income between wealthy and poor nations has widened sharply since trade barriers began falling. --- DISPARITY (n) = sự chênh lệch lớn; luôn hàm ý so sánh giữa hai bên; collocation "widening disparity", "income disparity".

6. After years of relying on overseas factories, several car makers are now pursuing reshoring, bringing production back to their home countries. --- RESHORING (n) = đưa sản xuất trở về nước sở tại; đối lập với "offshoring"; viết liền không gạch nối.

7. International organisations are working hard to eradicate extreme poverty within a generation. --- ERADICATE (v) = xoá bỏ hoàn toàn, tận diệt; dùng cho vấn đề nghiêm trọng (poverty, disease), không dùng cho mức giảm nhẹ.

8. Fund managers are pouring capital into emerging economies like Vietnam and Indonesia, hoping for high returns. --- EMERGING (adj) = mới nổi, đang phát triển nhanh; collocation cố định "emerging economies/markets".

9. To reduce overheads, the airline turned to outsourcing, hiring an external company abroad to handle all its customer-service calls. --- OUTSOURCING (n) = thuê ngoài; nếu ra nước ngoài cụ thể thì gọi là "offshore outsourcing".

10. Critics argue that global fast-food chains and shopping malls are driving the homogenisation of cities everywhere. --- HOMOGENISATION (n) = sự đồng nhất hoá, mất bản sắc riêng; chính tả Anh-Anh dùng "-isation"; collocation "cultural homogenisation".

11. Decades of trade liberalisation have opened domestic markets to fierce foreign competition. --- LIBERALISATION (n) = sự tự do hoá thương mại/kinh tế; collocation "trade/market liberalisation"; chính tả Anh-Anh "-isation".

12. Rather than a bilateral deal between just two countries, this new trade pact is multilateral, involving more than a dozen nations negotiating together. --- MULTILATERAL (adj) = đa phương, liên quan từ ba bên trở lên; đối lập với "bilateral" (song phương).
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: A lot of manufacturing has shifted to developing countries where labour is considerably cheaper.
Band 8: Offshore outsourcing enables firms to slash labour costs, albeit at the expense of local employment in their home markets.
2. Band 7: Trade disputes between nations can sometimes escalate into serious diplomatic conflict rather than fostering cooperation.
Band 8: Far from guaranteeing harmony, trade frictions can just as readily precipitate diplomatic conflict as they can cement mutual interdependence.
3. Band 7: Workers in developing nations are sometimes subjected to unfair and exploitative treatment by multinational corporations.
Band 8: Multinational corporations frequently exploit lax labour laws, resulting in exploitative labour practices that leave workers in developing nations acutely vulnerable.
4. Band 7: Many highly skilled professionals leave poorer countries in search of better-paid opportunities overseas.
Band 8: The severe brain drain deprives emerging economies of their most talented professionals, who are lured abroad by markedly better prospects.
5. Band 7: Because instant global communication connects everyone, the world increasingly resembles one closely knit community.
Band 8: With the internet connecting us instantly, it truly is a global village, in which geographic distance scarcely impedes the flow of information.
6. Band 7: Some countries have deliberately begun to separate their economies from rival powers for political reasons.
Band 8: Decoupling is no longer merely rhetorical; strategic disentanglement from rival economies is now being pursued as a matter of deliberate policy.
7. Band 7: Small local businesses find it difficult to compete fairly against huge multinational corporations.
Band 8: Small domestic businesses desperately need a level playing field if they are to compete on anything approaching equal terms with multinational giants.
8. Band 7: A single smartphone is typically designed in one country, built from components manufactured in several others, and finally assembled somewhere else entirely.
Band 8: A modern smartphone illustrates a global value chain: designed in one country, with components fabricated across several others and final assembly undertaken elsewhere still.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

Supply Chain Vulnerability: Events like the COVID-19 pandemic and the Suez Canal blockage exposed the extreme fragility of global interconnectedness, prompting a massive shift from offshoring to reshoring.
The Rise of the Global South (BRICS): Emerging economies (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa) are challenging the traditional economic hegemony of Western superpowers.
The Death of Local Industries: Unfettered free trade allows cheap, mass-produced foreign goods to flood the market, frequently bankrupting domestic artisans and farmers who cannot compete on price.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Free Trade vs. Protectionism

Arguments FOR Free Trade: Creates a win-win situation by lowering prices for consumers and opening massive new markets for exporters; encourages international diplomacy and peace (trading partners rarely go to war); promotes technological exchange.

Arguments FOR Protectionism: Imposing tariffs shields vulnerable domestic industries from cut-throat foreign competition; protects local jobs from being offshored to sweatshops in developing nations; ensures national security by maintaining independence in essential sectors (e.g., agriculture, energy).
Topic: The Impact of Multinational Corporations (MNCs)
Positives: They bring immense Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) into emerging economies; they build vital infrastructure and create thousands of jobs, raising the local standard of living.

Negatives: They often exploit lax labour laws and environmental regulations in poorer nations; their sheer financial power allows them to monopolise local markets, effectively killing off small domestic competitors.
Topic: Cultural Globalisation (Enrichment vs. Homogenisation)
Enrichment: Promotes cosmopolitanism, tolerance, and the sharing of diverse cuisines, art, and ideas, effectively bridging the gap between historically isolated societies.

Homogenisation: Leads to the erosion of indigenous heritage as global brands (e.g., fast-food chains, Hollywood movies) replace traditional cultural expressions, making every city in the world look identical.
(Câu chẻ giả - Cấu trúc ngữ pháp "sát thủ" (Band 8.0+) giúp bạn nhấn mạnh ý chính trong câu mở bài, câu chốt đoạn, hoặc khi đưa ra giải pháp trong IELTS Writing Task 2).

Model Answer (Band 7.5-8.0, ~270 words)

The brand I'd like to discuss is Samsung, the South Korean electronics conglomerate, which — in my considered view — has more profoundly reshaped Vietnam's economic trajectory over the past two decades than perhaps any other multinational. Samsung established its first manufacturing presence here in 2008, when it opened a $670 million mobile phone facility in Bac Ninh Province; what followed has been nothing short of transformative.

The brand currently operates six factories and one R&D centre, employing roughly 110,000 Vietnamese workers directly, with another 300,000 indirectly across its supply chain. Samsung Vietnam now accounts for approximately 20% of the country's total export revenue — a staggering concentration that has, for better or worse, decisively shaped national industrial policy.

The ways in which Samsung has shaped Vietnam operate on multiple registers. Firstly, what its arrival catalysed was the country's emergence as a credible alternative to China in the great reshoring and "China-plus-one" decoupling now reshaping global supply chains. Secondly, the firm's technical training programmes — including a $220 million R&D centre in Hanoi opened in 2022 — have measurably upgraded the local engineering talent pool. Thirdly, entire provinces have urbanised around Samsung's industrial parks, with all the attendant gains and growing pains that rapid agglomeration brings.

My assessment is cautiously positive but qualified. On the upside, GDP growth, infrastructure investment, and white-collar job creation are tangible. On the downside, dependence on a single foreign anchor tenant creates a kind of structural precarity — if Samsung relocates, the shock would be acute — and the value-added share captured locally remains modest.
All in all, Samsung exemplifies both the promise and the perils of late-stage industrialisation through foreign direct investment.

blocks.text: Q1: Has globalisation gone too far?

Point: I'd argue that globalisation hasn't so much "gone too far" as it has proceeded along an unbalanced trajectory — one that maximised efficiency gains while systematically neglecting distributional consequences and supply chain resilience.

Explain: The fundamental issue is that frictionless trade did deliver enormous aggregate welfare gains — roughly a billion people lifted out of extreme poverty since 1990 — but those gains were captured disproportionately by capital owners and emerging-market workers, while working-class communities in developed nations bore the brunt of deindustrialisation.

Example: The "China shock" literature by economist David Autor estimates that roughly 2.4 million American manufacturing jobs were lost between 1999 and 2011 due to import competition, with depressed regions never fully recovering. Concurrently, COVID-19 exposed the precarity of just-in-time supply chains, prompting a measurable shift towards reshoring — US semiconductor reshoring alone attracted $200 billion in CHIPS Act subsidies. Vietnam, by contrast, has been a clear beneficiary of decoupling, with FDI inflows hitting $36.6 billion in 2023.
Link: So rather than rolling back globalisation wholesale, what's needed is its rebalancing — combining open trade with stronger domestic safety nets and strategic supply chain diversification.
Q2: Should countries protect local industries?
Point: Protectionism, used judiciously and temporarily, can be defensible — particularly for nascent strategic sectors — though as a blanket policy it tends to do more harm than good.

Explain: The classic "infant industry" argument, articulated by Friedrich List in the 19th century, holds that emerging industries need temporary shielding to achieve scale economies before facing global competition. The difficulty is that targeted protection routinely becomes permanent rent-seeking, with politically connected firms capturing subsidies indefinitely.

Example: South Korea's post-war industrial policy — protecting chaebols like Hyundai and Samsung through tariffs and credit subsidies until they could compete globally — is the textbook success case, transforming the country from agrarian poverty into a high-tech powerhouse within four decades. Conversely, India's pre-1991 import-substitution regime produced decades of stagnation, where protected domestic firms had little incentive to innovate. Vietnam's current approach — selective FDI incentives combined with gradual tariff liberalisation under CPTPP — strikes a more pragmatic balance.
Link: So protectionism is a scalpel, not a hammer — appropriate for narrow strategic objectives but disastrous when applied indiscriminately to entire economies.
Q3: Is English-language dominance fair?

Point: The global ascendancy of English is, in strict terms, neither fair nor unfair — it's a historical contingency rooted in British imperialism and American post-war hegemony — but its practical effects do create genuine asymmetries that deserve scrutiny.

Explain: What English-language dominance does is confer a structural advantage on roughly 380 million native speakers, who can access global academia, business, and entertainment in their mother tongue, while the remaining 1.1 billion English users bear the cognitive and economic costs of operating in a second language. This creates measurable inequities in scientific publishing, diplomacy, and digital labour markets.

Example: A 2023 study in PLOS Biology found that non-native English-speaking scientists spend roughly 90% more time reading papers and twice as long writing them — a clear productivity tax. Concurrently, the rise of large language models like ChatGPT, trained overwhelmingly on English-language corpora, is amplifying rather than mitigating this asymmetry. That said, the universal lingua franca does have coordination benefits, and proposals to replace English with Esperanto or Mandarin have repeatedly failed.
Link: So while English dominance isn't going anywhere, robust support for multilingual education and AI-assisted translation can at least soften its inequitable edges.

Lecture title: "Global Value Chains, Decoupling and the Economics of Reshoring"
1. Section Type

IELTS Listening — Section 4 (academic monologue in international trade and economic geography, ~3:00 minutes). Single speaker (Professor Tomás Beltrán, School of International Trade and Development). Note-completion + multiple-choice hybrid.
2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

rows: the dispersed cross-border network producing a single finished good
the deliberate disentangling of two economies' trade and technology ties
the return of previously offshored manufacturing to the home country
the principle that nations should specialise in their relative strengths
relocating supply chains to politically allied jurisdictions

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas (before listening)
The lecturer will probably argue that hyper-globalisation is being unwound, not reversed.
Decoupling may be reframed as strategic, not merely protectionist.
Reshoring will likely be presented as economically costly yet politically attractive.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. Today's lecture revisits the architecture of contemporary trade through three contested concepts: global value chains, decoupling and reshoring. The post-1990s consensus, I will argue, is being deliberately dismantled.

> Consider, first, the global value chain — abbreviated GVC. A modern smartphone is designed in California, with semiconductors fabricated in Taiwan, displays in South Korea, rare earths refined in China, and final assembly in Vietnam. The Harvard economist Pol Antràs has shown that more than seventy percent of world trade now consists of intermediate inputs, not finished goods. Ricardo's classical comparative advantage has, in effect, been atomised across borders.

> Now, decoupling. The term entered policy vocabulary around 2018, principally to describe the strategic disentanglement of the United States and China in semiconductors, rare-earth minerals and artificial-intelligence chips. The US CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 allocated fifty-two billion dollars to onshore chip fabrication. The European Union followed with parallel legislation. Decoupling is no longer rhetorical; it is legislatively encoded.

> Finally, reshoring and its softer cousin, friend-shoring. Pandemic-era supply-chain ruptures, the Suez blockage of 2021 and the Russia-Ukraine war collectively exposed the fragility of just-in-time production. Yet the economics are sobering. Boston Consulting Group estimates that reshoring a typical electronics assembly line to the United States raises unit costs by twenty to forty percent. Consumers, in the end, foot the bill.

Now, that GVC participation chart will show you the aggregate trend, but I want to resist a tempting oversimplification before we read it — the idea that decoupling and reshoring are reversing globalisation. They are not, quite. What we are witnessing is better described as a reconfiguration, not a retreat. Trade is not shrinking so much as rerouting, and the geography of that rerouting is where the real story lies. [pause] Consider Mexico, which in 2023 overtook China as the largest source of US imports — that is not deglobalisation; that is globalisation finding a new map.

The economist Richard Baldwin has a useful frame here. He distinguishes the trade in goods from the trade in knowledge and services, and his point is that even as we re-shore physical assembly, the intangible flows — design, software, data, intellectual property — are accelerating and remain stubbornly global. You can repatriate a factory; you cannot easily repatriate a global engineering team coordinating in real time across twelve time zones. So the value chain is, um, splitting along a new seam: the atoms come home while the bits stay borderless.

And there is a strategic subtlety that the headline figures obscure. Friend-shoring assumes you can cleanly sort the world into trusted and untrusted partners — but supply chains are recursive. Your trusted Vietnamese assembler may depend on Chinese sub-components two tiers down the chain, invisible on the bill of materials. [pause] The Kearney reshoring index has flagged exactly this: apparent diversification at the surface can mask deepening concentration underneath. We may be buying the comfort of resilience without the substance of it.

So the paradox I named earlier — resilience versus affordability — turns out to have a third horn we cannot ignore: the sheer difficulty of even knowing how exposed you are. This is why the policy conversation we move to now cannot simply choose between openness and security, but must first ask whether…

> The synthesis is paradoxical: nations crave both resilience and affordability, but the two pull in opposite directions. Hyper-globalisation will not return, yet autarky remains impossible. Now, turning to figure five, which traces GVC participation rates since 1990…
5. Vocabulary Highlighted (band 8+ topic-specific)

6. Five Questions (≥3 paraphrase)
Q1. (Note completion — paraphrase)

(Answer: Antràs)
Q2. (MCQ — paraphrase)

A. assembly is concentrated in one country
B. comparative advantage has been atomised across multiple borders within a single product
C. semiconductors are produced exclusively in the US
D. the smartphone is no longer globally traded
(Answer: B)
Q3. (Short answer — paraphrase)

(Answer: fifty-two / 52)
Q4. (MCQ — paraphrase / inference)

A. is essentially cost-neutral
B. carries significant cost penalties ultimately passed on to consumers
C. lowers prices for households
D. has been abandoned by the US government
(Answer: B)
Q5. (Note completion — paraphrase)
The lecturer concludes that hyper-globalisation will not return, yet __________ remains impossible.
(Answer: autarky)
7. Listen-For Cues
Q1 cue: the institutional-eponym frame "The Harvard economist Pol __________ has shown that…" — the surname falls before the verb "has shown".
Q2 cue: the cumulative-example frame "designed in California… fabricated in Taiwan… assembly in Vietnam" — flags the dispersion thesis.
Q3 cue: the dollar-figure frame "allocated __________ billion dollars to onshore chip fabrication" — figure precedes "billion".
Q4 cue: the consequence pivot "Consumers, in the end, foot the bill" — signals the cost-incidence inference.
Q5 cue: the paradox signpost "The synthesis is paradoxical…" — answer falls after "yet" in the closing sentence.

The two maps depict the reconfiguration of a Western electronics multinational's supply-chain network between 2010 and 2024, charting the location of its manufacturing hubs, assembly plants and component flows.

(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~199 từ)

The two maps trace the reconfiguration of a Western electronics multinational's supply-chain network between 2010 and 2024, charting the dispersion of its manufacturing hubs, assembly plants and component flows.

Overall, the network underwent a striking geographical contraction and regionalisation: Chinese capacity was sharply pared back while North American and Indian footprints expanded, signalling a deliberate retreat from concentrated offshoring toward a resilience-oriented, regionalised model.

In 2010, the firm's production was conspicuously China-centred, with four of its six manufacturing hubs clustered there, flanked by lone hubs in Vietnam and Mexico and two assembly plants in Malaysia and Poland. Components threaded along extended trans-Pacific arrows toward Western consumer markets and Japan, epitomising the offshoring logic of the era.

By 2024, this geometry had been recast. Only two — visibly downsized — Chinese facilities survived, whereas fresh hubs had materialised in Texas, India and an enlarged Mexican site, complemented by a new Arizona assembly plant. The flows contracted in tandem, the trans-Pacific routes giving way to three compact regional clusters around North America, Southeast Asia and the EU. That the firm should reshore even as costs rose suggests a recalibration in which resilience, not cost minimisation, now governs the global value chain.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~272 words)

For four decades, globalisation has been hailed as a process that benefits everyone, yet a growing number of analysts argue that the gains have flowed disproportionately to wealthy nations. While there is real evidence of unequal benefits, I disagree that developing economies have been net losers, although the picture is undeniably mixed.

Those who support the critical view marshal compelling arguments. Multinational corporations have repeatedly relocated production to poorer countries to exploit lax labour laws, paying minimal wages while extracting substantial profits for headquarters in wealthier nations. It is the unequal terms of trade that, in their view, lock developing nations into low-value exports such as raw materials and basic textiles, which tends to entrench rather than narrow the income disparity. Furthermore, cultural homogenisation often erodes indigenous heritage as Western brands flood emerging markets.

On the other hand, the headline gains for developing countries are too large to dismiss. Hundreds of millions of people in East and Southeast Asia have escaped absolute poverty as a direct result of integration into global supply chains. Foreign direct investment has built modern infrastructure, transferred technology and created jobs that pay above local averages. What countries like Vietnam, India and Bangladesh have demonstrated is that strategic engagement with global trade can dramatically accelerate development, provided that domestic institutions are reasonably competent.

In conclusion, although globalisation has clearly produced winners and losers within every economy, the suggestion that it has benefited rich nations at the expense of poor ones tends to oversimplify a complex record. What developing countries require is fairer trade rules and a more level playing field, rather than a retreat from global engagement itself.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~287 words)

That globalisation has redistributed wealth on a planetary scale is uncontroversial; whether it has done so at the systematic expense of developing nations is far more contentious. Having weighed the evidence, I disagree with the strong version of the claim: while gains have plainly been uneven, the assertion that poor nations have been net losers does not survive scrutiny.

Critics raise serious points. Trade liberalisation has frequently locked developing economies into low-margin segments of global value chains, while multinational corporations exploit regulatory arbitrage to suppress wages and externalise environmental costs. So pronounced has this asymmetry been that some economists describe contemporary trade as a form of neo-colonial extraction. Moreover, the cultural hegemony of Western media risks homogenising indigenous traditions, eroding the soft power of smaller nations. None of these concerns is trivial.

Nevertheless, the macro-level record complicates the indictment. Roughly a billion people have moved out of extreme poverty since 1990, the bulk of them in countries that aggressively pursued export-led integration. What economies such as South Korea, Vietnam and Botswana illustrate is that, with competent industrial policy, globalisation can serve as a ladder rather than a trap. Recent trends only reinforce this point: the wave of reshoring and selective decoupling now sweeping advanced economies threatens precisely those developing nations that depend on access to Northern markets, which suggests that globalisation, far from being uniformly extractive, has long been a vital channel of upward mobility.

On balance, then, globalisation's benefits and harms are mediated by domestic institutions and bargaining power, not destiny. What the international system genuinely requires is fairer rules — on tax, intellectual property and climate finance — rather than withdrawal. Reform, not retreat, offers the most credible route to a more equitable global economy.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 huy động lexis Band 8 ('regulatory arbitrage', 'neo-colonial extraction', 'export-led integration', 'reshoring', 'decoupling', 'climate finance') và dẫn xu hướng đương đại (reshoring đe doạ nước phụ thuộc thị trường Bắc), nâng Task Response.

•  Band 8 đạt cohesion mượt với connector tinh tế ('complicates the indictment', 'far from being uniformly extractive') và khép bằng cleft tương phản 'Reform, not retreat', vượt rõ câu kết trực diện của Band 7.

title: Globalisation and Trade

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự phụ thuộc lẫn nhau giữa các quốc gia hoặc nền kinh tế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Global trade has rendered national economies profoundly **interdependent**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
inter- (giữa các bên) + dependence (phụ thuộc) → các nước dựa vào NHAU, không phải một chiều.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'interdependence' (phụ thuộc LẪN NHAU, hai chiều) với 'dependence' (phụ thuộc một chiều).
vocabulary.definition_en: the state in which two or more countries, economies, or people rely on each other
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phụ thuộc lẫn nhau (giữa các quốc gia, nền kinh tế)
vocabulary.example: Global trade has rendered national economies profoundly interdependent.
vocabulary.memory_hook: inter- (giữa các bên) + dependence (phụ thuộc) → các nước dựa vào NHAU, không phải một chiều.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chủ nghĩa bảo hộ mậu dịch, dùng thuế quan và hạn ngạch để bảo vệ ngành trong nước.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Protectionist** tariffs are frequently invoked to shield domestic industries from foreign competition.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
protect (bảo vệ) + -ionism (chủ nghĩa) → chính sách bảo vệ hàng nội địa khỏi hàng ngoại.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Protectionism' là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ chính sách; tính từ đi kèm là 'protectionist' (protectionist tariffs), không phải 'protectionism tariffs'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the policy of shielding domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs and quotas
vocabulary.definition_vi: chủ nghĩa bảo hộ (mậu dịch)
vocabulary.example: Protectionist tariffs are frequently invoked to shield domestic industries from foreign competition.
vocabulary.memory_hook: protect (bảo vệ) + -ionism (chủ nghĩa) → chính sách bảo vệ hàng nội địa khỏi hàng ngoại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quyền bá chủ, sự thống trị của một quốc gia hoặc nhóm xã hội đối với các nước khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some nations have embraced protectionism, challenging the **hegemony** of the dominant global superpowers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hy Lạp cổ: 'hegemon' = nước dẫn đầu liên minh → hegemony = quyền bá chủ, đứng đầu thiên hạ.
vocabulary.common_error: Phát âm dễ sai: trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết 2 /hɪˈɡem.ə.ni/, không phải /ˈhedʒ.ə.moʊ.ni/.
vocabulary.definition_en: the leadership or dominance of one country or social group over others
vocabulary.definition_vi: quyền bá chủ, sự thống trị (của một quốc gia hay nhóm)
vocabulary.example: Some nations have embraced protectionism, challenging the hegemony of the dominant global superpowers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hy Lạp cổ: 'hegemon' = nước dẫn đầu liên minh → hegemony = quyền bá chủ, đứng đầu thiên hạ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chuyển hoạt động sản xuất hoặc dịch vụ ra nước ngoài để giảm chi phí.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Offshore** outsourcing enables firms to slash costs, albeit at the expense of local employment.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
off + shore (bờ biển) → đưa việc 'ra khỏi bờ', sang bên kia đại dương.
collocations: a shift from offshoring to reshoring
vocabulary.common_error: 'Offshoring' (chuyển ra nước ngoài) khác 'outsourcing' (thuê ngoài, có thể vẫn trong nước); hai khái niệm hay bị dùng lẫn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the practice of basing some of a company's processes or services overseas to reduce costs
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuyển hoạt động sản xuất/dịch vụ ra nước ngoài (để giảm chi phí)
vocabulary.example: Offshore outsourcing enables firms to slash costs, albeit at the expense of local employment.
vocabulary.memory_hook: off + shore (bờ biển) → đưa việc 'ra khỏi bờ', sang bên kia đại dương.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự chênh lệch, bất bình đẳng lớn giữa các nhóm người hoặc khu vực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Unfettered trade liberalisation can exacerbate **disparities** between developed and developing nations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
dis- (khác biệt) + par (ngang bằng, như 'par' trong golf) → không ngang bằng → chênh lệch.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Disparity' luôn hàm ý sự CHÊNH LỆCH giữa hai bên, không dùng để chỉ một con số đơn lẻ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a great difference or inequality between people, regions, or groups
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự chênh lệch, sự bất bình đẳng lớn
vocabulary.example: Unfettered trade liberalisation can exacerbate disparities between developed and developing nations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: dis- (khác biệt) + par (ngang bằng, như 'par' trong golf) → không ngang bằng → chênh lệch.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đưa hoạt động sản xuất và dịch vụ trở về nước sở tại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Supply chain disruptions have also sparked a trend of **reshoring**, bringing factories back home.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (trở lại) + shore (bờ) → đưa nhà máy quay trở lại bờ nhà mình.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'reshoring' (đưa SẢN XUẤT về nước) với 're-shoring' theo nghĩa đen về bờ biển; đây là thuật ngữ kinh tế cố định, viết liền không gạch nối.
vocabulary.definition_en: the act of returning manufacturing operations and services to one's home country
vocabulary.definition_vi: đưa hoạt động sản xuất trở về nước sở tại
vocabulary.example: Supply chain disruptions have also sparked a trend of reshoring, bringing factories back home.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (trở lại) + shore (bờ) → đưa nhà máy quay trở lại bờ nhà mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Xoá bỏ hoàn toàn, tận diệt một vấn đề xã hội (nghèo đói, bệnh tật).

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> International charities desperately want to **eradicate** extreme poverty.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
e- (ra khỏi) + radic- (rễ, như 'radical, root') → nhổ tận gốc rễ → xoá bỏ hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Eradicate' mang nghĩa xoá bỏ TRIỆT ĐỂ, không dùng cho việc giảm nhẹ đơn thuần (nên dùng 'reduce' cho mức độ nhỏ hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: to destroy completely; to put an end to a social ill or problem
vocabulary.definition_vi: xoá bỏ hoàn toàn, tận diệt (nghèo đói, bệnh tật)
vocabulary.example: International charities desperately want to eradicate extreme poverty.
vocabulary.memory_hook: e- (ra khỏi) + radic- (rễ, như 'radical, root') → nhổ tận gốc rễ → xoá bỏ hoàn toàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mới nổi, đang phát triển nhanh chóng hướng tới hiện đại hoá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Investors are increasingly looking for lucrative opportunities in **emerging** economies like India and Brazil.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
e- (ra khỏi) + merge (chìm) → 'nổi lên khỏi mặt nước' → nền kinh tế đang trồi lên, bứt phá.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Emerging economy' (đang nổi lên, tăng trưởng nhanh) khác 'developing country' (đang phát triển nói chung, có thể chưa tăng trưởng nhanh).
vocabulary.definition_en: (of an economy or market) becoming prominent and developing rapidly toward modernisation
vocabulary.definition_vi: mới nổi, đang phát triển nhanh (nền kinh tế/thị trường)
vocabulary.example: Investors are increasingly looking for lucrative opportunities in emerging economies like India and Brazil.
vocabulary.memory_hook: e- (ra khỏi) + merge (chìm) → 'nổi lên khỏi mặt nước' → nền kinh tế đang trồi lên, bứt phá.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuê ngoài công ty hoặc cá nhân khác thực hiện công việc thay vì dùng nhân sự của mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company plans to **outsource** its IT department to India to save on labour costs.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
out (ra ngoài) + source (nguồn) → tìm nguồn lực bên ngoài công ty để làm việc.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Outsourcing' không nhất thiết ra nước ngoài (có thể thuê công ty trong nước); nếu ra nước ngoài thì gọi cụ thể là 'offshore outsourcing'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the practice of paying an outside company or individual to do work or provide services instead of using one's own staff
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuê ngoài (dịch vụ, sản xuất)
vocabulary.example: The company plans to outsource its IT department to India to save on labour costs.
vocabulary.memory_hook: out (ra ngoài) + source (nguồn) → tìm nguồn lực bên ngoài công ty để làm việc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình các nền văn hoá hoặc sản phẩm khác nhau trở nên ngày càng giống nhau, mất bản sắc riêng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Cultural **homogenisation** is an oft-cited, and much-lamented, by-product of globalisation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
homo- (giống nhau, như trong 'homogeneous') → mọi thứ trở nên giống nhau, mất bản sắc riêng.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh: 'homogenisation' (British) vs 'homogenization' (American, dùng -ize/-ization).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process by which distinct cultures or products become increasingly similar and lose their individual character
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự đồng nhất hoá (văn hoá, sản phẩm)
vocabulary.example: Cultural homogenisation is an oft-cited, and much-lamented, by-product of globalisation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: homo- (giống nhau, như trong 'homogeneous') → mọi thứ trở nên giống nhau, mất bản sắc riêng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình gỡ bỏ các rào cản của chính phủ đối với thương mại hoặc nền kinh tế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Unfettered trade **liberalisation** can exacerbate disparities between developed and developing nations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
liberal (tự do) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình làm cho thương mại được tự do hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-isation' (liberalisation), không phải '-ization' kiểu Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of removing government restrictions on trade or the economy
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tự do hoá (thương mại, kinh tế)
vocabulary.example: Unfettered trade liberalisation can exacerbate disparities between developed and developing nations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: liberal (tự do) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình làm cho thương mại được tự do hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính bóc lột, đối xử bất công để trục lợi từ sức lao động của người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Multinational corporations often exploit lax labour laws, resulting in **exploitative** labour practices in poorer nations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
exploit (khai thác, bóc lột) + -ative → mang bản chất bóc lột.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Exploitative' (tính từ, mang tính bóc lột) khác 'exploitable' (có thể khai thác được, không mang nghĩa xấu).
vocabulary.definition_en: treating someone unfairly in order to benefit from their work or resources
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính bóc lột
vocabulary.example: Multinational corporations often exploit lax labour laws, resulting in exploitative labour practices in poorer nations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: exploit (khai thác, bóc lột) + -ative → mang bản chất bóc lột.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đa phương, liên quan đến ba bên trở lên, đặc biệt trong hiệp định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Multilateral** trade agreements are designed to create a win-win situation for all participating countries.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
multi- (nhiều) + lateral (bên, phía) → nhiều phía cùng tham gia.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'multilateral' (nhiều bên, 3+) với 'bilateral' (song phương, 2 bên).
vocabulary.definition_en: involving three or more countries or parties, especially in an agreement
vocabulary.definition_vi: đa phương (liên quan đến nhiều bên)
vocabulary.example: Multilateral trade agreements are designed to create a win-win situation for all participating countries.
vocabulary.memory_hook: multi- (nhiều) + lateral (bên, phía) → nhiều phía cùng tham gia.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Con dao hai lưỡi, vừa có lợi vừa có hại cùng lúc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Globalisation's distributional effects are mediated by domestic institutions, making it **a double-edged sword** for developing economies.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thanh kiếm hai lưỡi (double-edged sword) chém được cả hai phía → vừa có lợi vừa gây hại.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là cụm cố định (idiom), không tách rời 'double' và 'edged'; luôn đi với mạo từ 'a'.
vocabulary.definition_en: something that has both significant advantages and significant disadvantages at the same time
vocabulary.definition_vi: con dao hai lưỡi (vừa lợi vừa hại)
vocabulary.example: Globalisation's distributional effects are mediated by domestic institutions, making it a double-edged sword for developing economies.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Thanh kiếm hai lưỡi (double-edged sword) chém được cả hai phía → vừa có lợi vừa gây hại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị soi xét, bị đưa ra xem xét kỹ lưỡng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The ethics of offshore outsourcing have **come under** intense **scrutiny** in recent years.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
scrutiny nghe như 'security check' kỹ lưỡng → 'come under scrutiny' = bị soi dưới kính lúp.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scrutiny' là danh từ không đếm được, không thêm 's' ('scrutinies' sai trong ngữ cảnh này).
vocabulary.definition_en: to start being examined or criticised very carefully
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị soi xét, bị đưa ra xem xét kỹ lưỡng
vocabulary.example: The ethics of offshore outsourcing have come under intense scrutiny in recent years.
vocabulary.memory_hook: scrutiny nghe như 'security check' kỹ lưỡng → 'come under scrutiny' = bị soi dưới kính lúp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chiến lược chuyển chuỗi cung ứng sang các quốc gia đồng minh chính trị đáng tin cậy, thay vì nơi có chi phí thấp nhất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Finally, reshoring and its softer cousin, **friend-shoring**: pandemic-era supply-chain ruptures exposed the fragility of just-in-time production.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
friend (bạn bè, đồng minh) + shoring (đặt sản xuất) → chỉ đặt nhà máy ở nước "bạn bè" đáng tin cậy.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Friend-shoring' (ưu tiên đồng minh chính trị) khác 'reshoring' (đưa hẳn về nước) — friend-shoring vẫn ở nước ngoài nhưng chọn đối tác tin cậy về địa chính trị.
vocabulary.definition_en: the practice of relocating supply chains to politically allied or trusted countries rather than the cheapest available location
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuyển chuỗi cung ứng sang các nước đồng minh chính trị (thay vì nơi rẻ nhất)
vocabulary.example: Finally, reshoring and its softer cousin, friend-shoring: pandemic-era supply-chain ruptures exposed the fragility of just-in-time production.
vocabulary.memory_hook: friend (bạn bè, đồng minh) + shoring (đặt sản xuất) → chỉ đặt nhà máy ở nước 'bạn bè' đáng tin cậy.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sân chơi bình đẳng, không bên nào có lợi thế bất công.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Small domestic businesses desperately need **a level playing field** to compete with foreign giants.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Sân bóng phải bằng phẳng (level) để hai đội thi đấu công bằng → sân chơi bình đẳng trong kinh doanh.
collocations: a level playing field for sb
compete on a level playing field
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này luôn đi với mạo từ 'a' và động từ thường là 'need/create/ensure a level playing field', không chia số nhiều 'fields'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which everyone has an equal chance of succeeding, with no side having an unfair advantage
vocabulary.definition_vi: sân chơi bình đẳng (không bên nào có lợi thế bất công)
vocabulary.example: Small domestic businesses desperately need a level playing field to compete with foreign giants.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Sân bóng phải bằng phẳng (level) để hai đội thi đấu công bằng → sân chơi bình đẳng trong kinh doanh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình huống mà tất cả các bên liên quan đều được lợi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Free trade agreements are designed to create **a win-win situation** for both participating countries.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
win + win (thắng + thắng) → cả hai bên đều thắng, không ai thua.
collocations: a win-win situation for both sides
vocabulary.common_error: 'Win-win' luôn viết có gạch nối và lặp từ 'win'; không viết 'winning-winning' hay 'win-to-win'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation or agreement that benefits everyone involved
vocabulary.definition_vi: tình huống đôi bên cùng có lợi
vocabulary.example: Free trade agreements are designed to create a win-win situation for both participating countries.
vocabulary.memory_hook: win + win (thắng + thắng) → cả hai bên đều thắng, không ai thua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng nhân tài, người có trình độ cao rời khỏi đất nước ra nước ngoài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The severe **brain drain** deprives emerging economies of their most talented professionals.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
brain (chất xám) + drain (chảy đi, như nước rút xuống cống) → nhân tài chảy ra nước ngoài.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Brain drain' là danh từ ghép không đếm được, không thêm 's'; đối lập với nó là 'brain gain', không phải 'brain fill'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the emigration of highly skilled or educated people from a country, usually to seek better opportunities abroad
vocabulary.definition_vi: chảy máu chất xám
vocabulary.example: The severe brain drain deprives emerging economies of their most talented professionals.
vocabulary.memory_hook: brain (chất xám) + drain (chảy đi, như nước rút xuống cống) → nhân tài chảy ra nước ngoài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thế giới được xem như một cộng đồng gắn kết chặt chẽ nhờ công nghệ truyền thông.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> With the internet connecting us instantly, it truly is **a global village**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thế giới (global) thu nhỏ lại như một ngôi làng (village) nơi ai cũng biết tin tức của nhau ngay lập tức.
collocations: the world as a global village
the idea of a global village
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm ẩn dụ này chỉ dùng để mô tả sự kết nối/giao tiếp toàn cầu, không dùng theo nghĩa đen về một ngôi làng thật.
vocabulary.definition_en: the world viewed as a single closely connected community due to advances in communication and travel
vocabulary.definition_vi: làng toàn cầu (thế giới như một cộng đồng gắn kết chặt chẽ)
vocabulary.example: With the internet connecting us instantly, it truly is a global village.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Thế giới (global) thu nhỏ lại như một ngôi làng (village) nơi ai cũng biết tin tức của nhau ngay lập tức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thu hẹp hoặc xoá bỏ khoảng cách giữa hai sự vật, nhóm người hoặc tình huống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Technological advancements help to **bridge the gap** between different nations and cultures.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Cây cầu (bridge) nối hai bờ sông cách xa nhau → bridge the gap = nối liền khoảng cách.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Bridge' ở đây là động từ (nối liền), khác với danh từ 'bridge' (cây cầu); không dùng 'gap the bridge'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to reduce or eliminate the difference between two things, groups, or situations
vocabulary.definition_vi: thu hẹp khoảng cách, kết nối những khác biệt
vocabulary.example: Technological advancements help to bridge the gap between different nations and cultures.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Cây cầu (bridge) nối hai bờ sông cách xa nhau → bridge the gap = nối liền khoảng cách.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chế độ tự cung tự cấp, không phụ thuộc vào thương mại với nước khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The interconnectedness of the modern world has proved that no nation can survive in **autarky**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
auto- (tự thân) + -archy (như trong hierarchy) → tự mình lo liệu mọi thứ, không cần ai.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'autarky' (tự cung tự cấp kinh tế) với 'autocracy' (chế độ chuyên chế, độc tài) — hai từ phát âm gần giống nhưng nghĩa hoàn toàn khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being economically self-sufficient and not dependent on trade with other countries
vocabulary.definition_vi: chế độ tự cung tự cấp (không phụ thuộc thương mại quốc tế)
vocabulary.example: The interconnectedness of the modern world has proved that no nation can survive in autarky.
vocabulary.memory_hook: auto- (tự thân) + -archy (như trong hierarchy) → tự mình lo liệu mọi thứ, không cần ai.

Sự tách rời có chủ đích giữa hai nền kinh tế về thương mại và công nghệ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Decoupling** is no longer rhetorical; it is legislatively encoded through acts such as the US CHIPS and Science Act.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (tách ra) + coupling (ghép đôi, như toa tàu nối nhau) → tháo rời hai nền kinh tế từng gắn kết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Decoupling' là quá trình có CHỦ ĐÍCH, mang tính chiến lược/chính trị, khác với 'disconnection' ngẫu nhiên.
vocabulary.definition_en: the deliberate disentangling of two economies' trade and technology ties
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tách rời (chủ động) giữa hai nền kinh tế về thương mại/công nghệ
vocabulary.example: Decoupling is no longer rhetorical; it is legislatively encoded through acts such as the US CHIPS and Science Act.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (tách ra) + coupling (ghép đôi, như toa tàu nối nhau) → tháo rời hai nền kinh tế từng gắn kết.

Mạng lưới xuyên biên giới các giai đoạn và doanh nghiệp tham gia sản xuất ra một sản phẩm hoàn chỉnh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A modern smartphone illustrates a **global value chain**: designed in California, with semiconductors fabricated in Taiwan and final assembly in Vietnam.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
value (giá trị) được thêm vào ở mỗi mắt xích (chain) qua từng quốc gia → chuỗi giá trị toàn cầu.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Global value chain' (chuỗi các giai đoạn tạo GIÁ TRỊ gia tăng, khái niệm kinh tế học) thường bị dùng lẫn với 'supply chain' (chuỗi CUNG ỨNG vật lý) dù có liên quan chặt chẽ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the dispersed cross-border network of stages and firms involved in producing a single finished good
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuỗi giá trị toàn cầu
vocabulary.example: A modern smartphone illustrates a global value chain: designed in California, with semiconductors fabricated in Taiwan and final assembly in Vietnam.
vocabulary.memory_hook: value (giá trị) được thêm vào ở mỗi mắt xích (chain) qua từng quốc gia → chuỗi giá trị toàn cầu.
